description: How the web really works: clients, servers, and the conversation between them.

screens.body: Every time you open a site, a conversation happens: your browser (the client) sends a request — 'give me this page' — and a server sends back a response. Request, response, repeat. That loop is the entire web.
screens.heading: How the web actually works
screens.keyPoint: Request, response, repeat — that's the web.

screens.body: The client is what the user sees and touches: HTML, CSS, JavaScript running in the browser. The server is the brain: it holds the data, runs the logic, checks who's allowed in. They live on different computers and talk over the internet.

options: Client = browser UI, server = data and logic
check.question: Client vs server:

screens.heading: Client vs server

screens.body: Front-end frameworks (React, Vue) help you build the client: components, pages, interactions. Back-end frameworks (Express, Django) help you build the server: routes, databases, auth. Your course compares them so you can pick the right tool per side.
screens.heading: Front-end vs back-end frameworks

screens.body: You type a URL. The browser finds the server (DNS), opens a connection, and sends an HTTP request. The server figures out what you asked for, maybe queries a database, and sends back a response — HTML, or JSON data. The browser renders it. All in milliseconds.
screens.heading: The request journey

screens.body: The front-end and back-end agree on an API: a set of URLs (endpoints), what data to send, and what comes back. It's a contract. As long as both sides honor it, either side can change its internals freely.

options: A contract both sides agree on
check.question: An API is…

screens.heading: APIs: the contract
screens.keyPoint: Agree on the contract, change the insides.

screens.body: Data lives in a database behind the server. The client NEVER talks to the database directly — it asks the server, and the server asks the database. That one rule is half of web security.

check.question: How does the client reach the database?

screens.heading: Where data lives

screens.body: Think about SwiftGigs: your React app is the client. Your server (or Supabase) is the back-end. When someone posts a task, the app sends a request, the server saves it to the database and sends back confirmation. You're already living this architecture.
